name: Small modular nuclear reactors
summary: Smaller reactor designs aim to deliver factory-repeatable nuclear power or heat with less capital committed to each unit.
useCase: A utility adds several standardised reactors over time near an industrial site instead of financing one very large unit at once.
whyNow: The useful signal is progress through licensing, financing, fuel qualification and actual construction. The OECD NEA dashboard expanded from 42 assessed designs in 2023 to 74 in 2025, but that is an expanding assessment universe, not an increase in operating plants. The 2025 NEA review identified seven designs either operating or under construction. Its September 2026 digital edition provides a more current project-by-project readiness view. Demand from utilities and large electricity buyers improves the opportunity, while the IEA cautions that policy, regulation and delivery must align. Small size alone does not remove first-of-a-kind cost, waste, security, skilled-workforce or fuel constraints.

mainstream.scope: Repeat commercial orders for a small number of qualified designs in established nuclear countries; not mass global replacement of large reactors.
mainstream.rationale: First commercial deployments around 2030 need operating evidence before repeat fleets become routine. Successful early projects could support serial procurement in the early-to-mid 2030s. Delays in licensing, construction economics or specialist fuel can push broad adoption past 2035. The IEA’s 2050 scenarios span 40–120 GW, illustrating the policy sensitivity.

metric.name: SMR designs assessed in the NEA dashboard
metric.scope: Research/readiness coverage proxy; not reactors built, MW operating, sales or adoption.
metric.limitations: The assessed universe expands and eligibility changes, so the increase cannot be interpreted as deployment growth. The 2026 79-design figure is the digital dashboard snapshot; 129 designs were being tracked in its wider universe. No comparable full-year global operating SMR series was established here.
metric.futureNote: No defensible comparable external deployment forecast found. The separate maturity path is an analyst scenario, not measured adoption.

milestones.text: No harmonised annual SMR deployment series was identified in the selected dashboard sources; design development was pre-serial-commercialisation.
Early technology and licensing work cannot be equated with routine factory production; no comparable annual deployment value retained.
The first two NEA dashboard volumes assessed 42 designs against technology and commercial-readiness dimensions.
The second edition expanded to 56 assessed designs.
The third edition assessed 74 designs; seven were operating or under construction, a combined category.
NEA launched digital dashboard edition 4.0 on 28 September; the digital platform reported 79 assessed designs. This is a readiness update, not 79 operating reactors.

tailwinds: Firm-power demand and fleet replacement create identifiable customers.
Standardised designs can spread engineering cost over repeat projects if orders materialise.
Established nuclear supply chains offer a base for manufacturing and operations.
bottlenecks: First-of-a-kind costs and financing may offset the advantage of smaller unit size.
Some advanced designs require scarce qualified fuel and entirely new supply chains.
A memorandum or design approval is several major gates away from commercial electricity.
watchMetrics: Number of reactors with full funding, construction permits and physical first concrete.
First-unit actual construction cost per kW and schedule versus the investment case.
Binding repeat orders, fuel deliveries and sustained operating performance.
